items.title: Aispace launches secure temporary file sharing CLI for AI agents and humans with expiring links and optional local encryption [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Aispace has released an open-source command-line interface designed for secure, temporary file sharing between AI agents and human users. The tool supports expiring links, predictable JSON output, and optional local age X25519 encryption to maintain privacy and control over shared files. The client is built for automation with features like stable exit codes, streaming uploads, and no interactive prompts, making it suitable for integration with AI workflows. It offers configurable file expiration, download limits, authenticated handoffs, and encrypted storage, while the hosted service operates separately from the client repository. The project includes documentation, integration examples, and compatibility with various platforms and agent runtimes.

items.title: Brw launches as a browser alternative to Claude Chrome with fewer interaction turns and tokens, using stable references for agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Brw is a new browser project introduced as an alternative to Claude Chrome, aiming to improve efficiency by requiring fewer interaction turns and tokens for the same tasks. Unlike Claude Chrome, Brw's agents operate from stable references rather than fresh screenshots each turn, potentially enhancing performance and stability. A public benchmark comparing the two browsers is planned to provide further evaluation.

items.title: Anthropic AI formalizes Fermat's Last Theorem proof in 11 days using Claude chatbot, completing a task expected to take humans 10 years [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic AI used its Claude chatbot to formalize the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem into computer-verifiable code within 11 days, a process that mathematicians anticipated would require a decade. This achievement marks the first time the 13-million-line proof, originally completed by Andrew Wiles in 1994, has been fully formalized in a programming language for automated verification. The breakthrough demonstrates AI's growing capability in advanced mathematical reasoning and formal proof verification, potentially accelerating future mathematical research and validation. Experts say this progress could lead AI to scrutinize extensive mathematical knowledge and identify errors in established results, a development once considered a distant possibility.

items.title: Arm CEO says chip shortage is delaying AI-driven cancer cure development amid growing demand for AI data center hardware [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Rene Haas, CEO of Arm Holdings, stated that artificial intelligence could find a cure for cancer beyond human capability within our lifetimes, but current chip shortages are slowing progress. The shortage affects the availability of hardware needed to advance AI technologies in healthcare and data centers. Haas highlighted that while AI modeling of complex biological processes is currently limited, improvements in computing power and data will enable breakthroughs. He also noted strong demand for Arm-designed chips in AI data centers worldwide but expressed skepticism about the UK manufacturing its own chips due to high costs and resource needs. Experts emphasize that the future of medical AI depends on quality data rather than just computing scale.

items.title: OpenCode launches X analytics leaderboard to highlight top contributors and boost community engagement
items.content_text: The OpenCode team has introduced an analytics leaderboard on the X platform designed to showcase top contributors and provide data-driven insights to enhance community interaction. The leaderboard aims to foster engagement by tracking and displaying user activity and influence within the platform.

items.title: Denzel explains the concept of AI 'slop' and its significance in artificial intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Denzel provided an explanation of AI "slop," detailing what it entails and why it matters in the context of artificial intelligence. The discussion highlights the nuances and implications of this concept within AI development and usage.

items.title: Analysis finds 21% of robots.txt user-agent lines on top 5,000 sites use invalid tokens that do not name intended crawlers, causing parsing and enforcement issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study of robots.txt files on the top 5,000 websites found that 582 sites (21.4%) include user-agent lines with values that do not conform to the RFC 9309 grammar, which only allows letters, hyphens, and underscores. This causes many user-agent tokens containing digits or spaces to be truncated or misread by standard parsers like Google's, leading to rules that either apply to nonexistent crawlers or merge unintentionally with other rules. For example, "AI2Bot" is parsed as "AI," which may not correspond to the intended crawler. The research highlights that while some crawlers may honor the full string they identify with, standard parsers do not, creating inconsistencies in how robots.txt directives are interpreted. The issue arises partly because crawler names often include characters disallowed by the standard grammar. The study recommends not deleting these lines but instead using broader disallow rules combined with exact tokens for allowed crawlers to ensure intended behavior. Tools are available to check robots.txt files against this parsing logic.

items.title: AI-driven software development is causing over-engineering and excessive production of code, tests, policies, and governance artifacts, raising concerns about maintenance and sustainability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A recent analysis highlights that artificial intelligence has drastically reduced the cost of building software, leading to an overproduction of technical and organizational artifacts such as code, tests, documentation, and governance structures. This surge in output, exemplified by a system called Wheelhouse managing thousands of commits and complex agent roles, shows AI's capacity to accelerate development but also creates challenges in understanding, maintaining, and pruning these artifacts. The case of Wheelhouse, which supports the game Wyvern, illustrates how AI agents generate extensive legal and operational frameworks to coordinate their actions, effectively creating a self-governing system. While this production is useful and improves reliability, it also reflects a shift where creating new components is cheap but managing their lifecycle remains costly, potentially leading to inefficiencies and resource strain in software projects and organizations.

items.title: Discussion on Hacker News reveals unease about rapid AI advancements and lack of coordinated pause efforts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A Hacker News thread captures growing concern among technology enthusiasts about the accelerating development of artificial intelligence and the absence of coordinated efforts to pause or regulate its progress. Participants express worry over the potential arrival of advanced AI systems within a year and the unresolved challenges of alignment and safety. The discussion highlights skepticism toward dismissing warnings from leading AI researchers as mere hype, emphasizing the tangible capabilities already observed in daily life. Contributors fear the rush toward recursive self-improvement driven by competitive pressures among AI labs, and the profound societal changes that may follow, raising concerns for those unaware of these developments and their implications.

items.title: llm software updates to version 0.35 with support for OpenAI's new GPT-6 Astra model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The llm software has been updated to version 0.35, adding support for OpenAI's new GPT-6 Astra model. This update was announced on September 7, 2026, by Simon Willison on his weblog, highlighting the integration of the latest OpenAI model into the llm framework.

items.title: VLDB revisits the Dataflow Model, assessing its impact on streaming analytics and database integration over 11 years
items.content_text: The paper "The Dataflow Model Revisited" reflects on the original Dataflow Model introduced 11 years ago, which addressed unbounded, out-of-order data and proposed a unified approach for balancing correctness, latency, and cost in batch and streaming data processing. The authors evaluate which aspects of their model have endured, such as the importance of event time and strong consistency, and which parts, like windowing and triggering, were less successful or overly complex. They also highlight the convergence of streams and tables as different views of the same data and note that many streaming analytics mechanisms evolved from traditional database techniques like SQL and incremental view maintenance. The authors discuss how the debate between batch and streaming processing was largely semantic and observe that low-latency demands have split along traditional OLTP and OLAP lines. They propose a new framing for streaming analytics and consider the possibility that streaming may eventually disappear as a distinct concept beyond analytics. This retrospective offers insights into the evolution of streaming data processing and its integration with established database principles.

items.title: Meta's AI crawler caused database overload on Usero by repeatedly hitting dynamic URLs without cookies, prompting Usero to implement bot detection and query optimizations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Usero experienced database overload due to Meta's AI crawler repeatedly accessing the /__manifest endpoint and generating numerous unique URLs by receiving new anonymous client IDs on each request. The crawler's behavior caused excessive database queries, leading to performance issues and error alerts. Usero identified the crawler through Cloudflare logs and user agent analysis, confirming it originated from Meta Platforms Ireland. The root cause involved the crawler discarding cookies, which triggered the generation of new client IDs embedded in URLs that the crawler then followed extensively. This led to multiple database queries per page load, especially on the integrations page, which lacked authentication and performed several database lookups before returning a 404 error. Additionally, requests to custom domains not recognized by Usero caused further unnecessary database lookups. To address the issue without blocking the crawler, Usero implemented bot detection using Cloudflare's verified bot categories and user agent checks to prevent bots from receiving anonymous IDs or setting cookies. The integrations page was modified to avoid database queries for bots, and custom domain lookups were optimized to check request paths before querying the database. These changes reduced the crawler's impact while allowing it to continue indexing the site.

items.title: Researchers use LLM-guided evolutionary algorithms to break 10 Packomania circle packing records with under $28 in computational cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed Discovery Loop, a system that uses a large language model to iteratively improve optimization algorithms for circle packing. Applied to the Packomania benchmark, it improved the best known solutions for 10 problem sizes between 101 and 114 circles, achieving 2.4% to 5.4% gains over prior records within 15 iterations and at a total LLM cost of $27.72. The results have been independently accepted by the Packomania community. The system starts from a simple seed solver and proposes algorithmic improvements guided by a scoreboard and history of prior ideas, with each candidate evaluated by an independent verifier. The study also analyzes cost-efficiency dynamics and introduces an adaptive plateau-detection mechanism, highlighting potential for democratizing automated scientific discovery in optimization problems.

items.title: Elevarq releases Analyzer 1.0 integrating LLM for PostgreSQL analysis but restricts it from determining factual findings [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Elevarq has launched Analyzer 1.0, a tool that integrates a large language model (LLM) to assist with PostgreSQL database investigation by explaining findings derived from deterministic analysis. The system collects evidence from PostgreSQL, establishes findings through deterministic methods, and uses the LLM only to explain those findings rather than to decide their truth, ensuring recommendations are evidence-based and reliable. The Analyzer runs locally within the user's environment to keep telemetry private and does not make automatic changes to databases, instead generating implementation-ready tickets for human review. This approach addresses risks of plausible but unsupported explanations by limiting the LLM's role to explanation, not diagnosis, emphasizing that findings must be grounded in concrete evidence rather than model-generated hypotheses.

items.title: TechCrunch publishes glossary of key AI terms including opaque recurrence, AGI, AI agents, and chain-of-thought reasoning to clarify emerging AI language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: TechCrunch has compiled a glossary defining important AI terms that have emerged alongside rapid advancements in the field, such as opaque recurrence, artificial general intelligence (AGI), AI agents, and chain-of-thought reasoning. The glossary aims to help readers, developers, and investors understand the evolving vocabulary used in AI discussions and product development. The glossary explains concepts like AGI, which refers to AI systems capable of outperforming humans at most economically valuable tasks, and AI agents, which are autonomous tools that perform multistep tasks beyond basic chatbots. It also covers technical terms such as API endpoints and coding agents, which automate software development tasks. TechCrunch plans to update the glossary regularly to keep pace with ongoing developments in AI technology and terminology.

items.title: Microsoft says ASCII smuggling technique used to evade phishing detection after originating in AI prompt injection attacks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Microsoft reports that ASCII smuggling, a technique first seen in AI prompt injection attacks, is now being employed in phishing campaigns to bypass security filters. This method manipulates ASCII characters to make phishing attempts harder to detect and block, posing new challenges for cybersecurity defenses.

items.title: Simon Willison launches a web-based video compressor using WebAssembly FFMPEG built by Claude Fable 5.1 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Simon Willison created a web tool to optimize video files using the WebAssembly version of FFMPEG, developed with assistance from Claude Fable 5.1 in Claude Code for web. The tool allows users to generate multiple compressed versions of a video with different presets for resolution, quality, and audio settings. The compressor was built to optimize a short demo video of Simon's Equal Earth animation recorded on his phone, enabling efficient publishing on his blog. The interface provides options such as encoder speed, H.264 profile, frame rate limits, metadata stripping, and audio control, with results showing significant size reductions across various presets.

items.title: Latent Space launches Frontier AEO Tracker analyzing Astra and other frontier models' product recommendations across 161 categories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Latent Space has introduced the Frontier AEO Tracker, a project that examines Answer Extraction and Opinion (AEO) trends by analyzing recommendations from Astra and six other frontier AI models across 161 categories. The tracker evaluates model preferences, biases, and confidence levels, providing insights into dominant products and shifts in model choices over time. The methodology extends previous work by running multiple prompt variations and scoring recommendations with a proprietary AEO score that accounts for positive and negative mentions. The analysis reveals patterns such as model-specific biases in coding agent recommendations and differences in source usage between model generations. The project also includes detailed reports on model transitions and a public interactive game to explore alignment with the data. Latent Space invites further input and business inquiries to expand this research.

items.title: Simon Willison uses GPT-6 Astra to create an animated D3 transition between Mercator and Equal Earth map projections following UN vote [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Simon Willison explored the Equal Earth map projection, recently voted on at the UN, by using GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT Work to build an animated transition between the Mercator and Equal Earth projections with D3. This project demonstrates a visual comparison of the two map projections using modern AI and web technologies.

items.title: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over alleged copyright infringement [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Seattle Times and Newsday have filed lawsuits against OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging unauthorized use of their copyrighted content. The legal action centers on claims that the AI companies used proprietary material without permission in training their models. The lawsuits highlight ongoing concerns about copyright and data usage in AI development.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate trusting-trust attack on entire Linux distribution via binary manipulation of GNU strip in NixOS build
items.content_text: Researchers have extended Ken Thompson's trusting-trust attack beyond compilers by manipulating the GNU strip utility's binaries to implant a backdoor that propagates through the NixOS Linux distribution build process. This attack modifies ELF files to persist malicious payloads across generations of the strip utility, ultimately backdooring nearly every binary in the final graphical installer without detection. The attack was successfully demonstrated on a real nixpkgs revision, showing that a single tampered strip binary in the bootstrap seed can infect subsequent builds and survive beyond the dependency closure. This reveals a broader threat vector in software supply chains, where build utilities not inspecting source code can still be exploited to compromise entire distributions.

items.title: Anthropic Labs launches Claude Design, a new AI design tool
items.content_text: Anthropic Labs has introduced Claude Design, a new product aimed at enhancing AI-driven design capabilities. This launch represents the company's latest effort to expand its AI tool offerings. Details about the features and intended applications of Claude Design have not been specified in the announcement.

items.title: OpenAI, WAN-IFRA, and AIRPPU launch AI program to support independent journalism in Ukraine amid ongoing conflict [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI, WAN-IFRA, and the Association of Independent Regional Press Publishers of Ukraine (AIRPPU) have announced a joint initiative to help Ukrainian news organizations adopt AI technologies to enhance innovation, resilience, and sustainability during the ongoing conflict. The program includes the Newsroom AI Masterclass Series and Newsroom AI Catalyst, which provide training, expert guidance, and OpenAI API credits to selected Ukrainian publishers. The initiative aims to improve editorial workflows, audience engagement, revenue generation, and operational efficiency by integrating AI-driven solutions tailored to the needs of independent newsrooms. The program builds on WAN-IFRA's global efforts to support AI adoption in journalism and OpenAI's partnerships with news organizations worldwide. The Newsroom AI Masterclass Series began in August 2026, with the Newsroom AI Catalyst launching in September 2026.

items.title: Report: Anthropic signs $517 billion in compute deals following Dario Amodei's warnings about reckless AI risk [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has reportedly secured $517 billion in compute contracts after its co-founder Dario Amodei cautioned competitors about the dangers of reckless risk-taking in AI development. This move highlights the company's aggressive investment in computational resources amid growing concerns over AI safety. Dario Amodei's warnings emphasize the need for caution in AI advancement, contrasting with Anthropic's substantial compute commitments that may influence the competitive landscape and risk management approaches within the AI industry.

items.title: Zhou Yu presents simulation-driven automated testing and evaluation methods to advance AI agents from demo to production, highlighting Columbia and Arklex AI's use of synthetic personas and CI/CD pipelines [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Zhou Yu discusses why most AI agents remain in the demo phase and explains how simulation-driven testing can address compliance and reliability challenges to enable production deployment. She highlights techniques used by Columbia University and Arklex AI, including synthetic user personas, trajectory entropy, and automated continuous integration and delivery pipelines, to evaluate multi-turn conversational agents and identify edge cases before deployment. Yu illustrates these methods through applications such as consumer-facing shopping agents used by Walmart and Amazon, emphasizing how enriched interactions and tool integrations improve agent performance. Her approach aims to scale self-learning workflows and improve the reliability of AI agents in real-world production environments.

items.title: Ars Technica reports on the complex corporate structure behind a $3.2 billion AI data center in New York, highlighting unclear safety and accountability amid a recent fire [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A fire at the Lake Mariner AI data center in Somerset, New York, revealed significant safety and accountability issues due to the involvement of multiple companies in the $3.2 billion project. The data center, owned and operated by TeraWulf on land leased from a company owned by its CEO, is also linked to Fluidstack, Google, and Anthropic, complicating responsibility for operational safety and emergency preparedness. Local firefighters faced challenges during the fire due to a lack of working alarms, suppression systems, and accessible safety documents. Despite TeraWulf's claims of responsibility for safety measures and subsequent improvements, some safety concerns remain unresolved. The incident underscores broader issues in the AI data center boom, where legal, operational, financial, and reputational responsibilities are often diffuse, raising questions about accountability, community impact, and promised economic benefits.

items.title: Google partners with Cathay Pacific to trial AI-powered contrail avoidance on ultra-long-haul Asia-Pacific flights, reducing warming impact by 40% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google is collaborating with Cathay Pacific to test AI technology that helps pilots avoid creating heat-trapping contrails by making small altitude adjustments on ultra-long-haul flights in the Asia-Pacific region. Early trials involving over 80 flights have shown a 40% reduction in the climate impact of contrails, which contribute significantly to aviation's overall warming effect. The system uses AI predictions, satellite imagery, and weather data to identify contrail-forming zones, providing flight teams with actionable altitude change recommendations before and during flights without affecting safety or passenger experience. This trial builds on previous efforts in the US and North Atlantic and aims to scale contrail avoidance as a practical, cost-effective method to reduce aviation's climate footprint in the world's fastest-growing aviation market.

items.title: Elon Musk's xAI loses second legal attempt to block Minnesota's ban on AI nudify apps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Elon Musk's AI company xAI has lost its second bid to prevent Minnesota from enforcing a ban on AI-powered nudify applications. The legal defeat means the state can continue restricting apps that use AI to alter images to create nude representations without consent. The case highlights ongoing regulatory challenges for AI technologies that manipulate images, with Minnesota taking a firm stance against such applications to protect privacy and prevent misuse. xAI's repeated legal efforts indicate the company's interest in contesting these restrictions but so far without success.

items.title: DeepMind launches WeatherNext 3, an hourly weather forecasting model using raw satellite imagery to track fast-changing conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: DeepMind has introduced WeatherNext 3, a new weather forecasting model that generates hourly forecasts by directly analyzing raw satellite imagery. This approach allows the model to provide timely updates on rapidly changing weather events such as rain and snow. Unlike previous models, WeatherNext 3's use of raw satellite data enhances its ability to track and predict short-term weather variations more accurately.

items.title: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement over AI training data use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The Seattle Times and Newsday have filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging that their journalism was used without permission to train AI models and that the AI often reproduces passages from their reporting. The lawsuit seeks the destruction of any copies of their works held by the companies, including training datasets and AI models incorporating their content. This legal action follows similar suits from other publishers and is part of a broader dispute over AI's impact on news organizations' subscription revenues.

items.title: Google DeepMind Accelerator backs 16 Asia-Pacific AI projects tackling climate, agriculture, and biodiversity challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google has selected 16 organizations across Asia-Pacific for its inaugural DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet program, supporting startups, nonprofits, and research teams using AI to address environmental issues. These projects focus on biodiversity monitoring, sustainable agriculture, and carbon solutions, receiving expert mentorship and access to advanced AI tools over three months to help scale their impact. The cohort includes groups working on AI-powered bioacoustics for biodiversity, satellite data for mangrove monitoring, AI-driven pest and weather guidance for farmers, and platforms for carbon credit verification. The program aims to accelerate innovative AI applications that contribute to environmental sustainability and climate resilience in the region.

items.title: Fluidstack leads Anthropic's $50 billion compute infrastructure build-out for AI development [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Fluidstack is spearheading the construction of a $50 billion compute infrastructure for Anthropic, supporting the company's AI development efforts. This large-scale build-out aims to provide the necessary computational resources for Anthropic's advanced AI models and research. The project represents a significant investment in AI hardware capacity, reflecting the growing demand for high-performance computing in the AI industry. Fluidstack's role involves managing and deploying the infrastructure to meet Anthropic's ambitious compute requirements.

items.title: OpenAI reports progress on automated AI researchers using coding agents to accelerate research and experiment velocity under human supervision [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has reached its goal of deploying an automated research intern capable of performing well-defined research tasks under human direction, marking significant progress toward creating a fully automated AI researcher by March 2028. Researchers at OpenAI are increasingly using coding agents to handle complex tasks, contributing to faster code development and more experiments, which is accelerating AI research within the organization. The company emphasizes that human researchers still set priorities and make critical decisions, and that safety and alignment remain central to development efforts. Following a recent security incident, OpenAI paused some training activities to enhance safeguards and monitoring. The organization advocates for transparency and public tracking of progress toward robust AI systems, aiming to balance rapid research advancement with responsible governance and safety measures.

items.title: Google DeepMind launches WeatherNext 3, an AI weather model using real-time satellite data for hourly, high-resolution global forecasts integrated into Google Search, Maps, and Cloud [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Google DeepMind has introduced WeatherNext 3, an advanced AI model that delivers more accurate and higher-resolution weather forecasts by leveraging real-time satellite data instead of traditional physics simulations. The model provides hourly updates with five times sharper spatial resolution, improving localized predictions for temperature, precipitation, and wind patterns worldwide. WeatherNext 3 is now integrated into Google Search, Maps, Gemini, and Google Cloud, enhancing weather information accessibility for users and developers. The model generates forecasts at multiple spatial resolutions, including 5 kilometers for key surface variables, enabling detailed visualization of local topography and weather events. Unlike previous models relying on numerical weather prediction data with six-hour delays, WeatherNext 3 learns directly from live satellite observations, allowing it to track fast-changing weather conditions with greater precision. This advancement supports better planning in sectors such as agriculture, renewable energy, and daily activities by providing timely and reliable weather information globally.

items.title: xAI launches Grok Bot AI teammates designed to complete tasks autonomously
items.content_text: xAI has introduced Grok Bot, an AI-powered teammate designed to autonomously finish work tasks. This development aims to enhance productivity by integrating AI agents that can assist or complete assignments independently.

items.title: OpenAI's Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki warns of rapidly advancing AI capabilities and calls for stronger safeguards and international coordination [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI, reflects on the rapid progress in AI reasoning models since 2023, highlighting their growing role in the economy, science, and computer security. He expresses concern about the potential for recursive self-improvement and the challenges of aligning increasingly intelligent systems with human values. Pachocki emphasizes that AI development is driven primarily by scaling computational power, resulting in complex systems that are difficult to fully understand. He calls for extreme caution and broader interventions beyond technical solutions, including international cooperation, to manage the risks posed by advanced AI systems.

items.title: Judge upholds Minnesota's ban on AI-generated nudity in case against xAI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A judge has maintained Minnesota's legal ban on AI-generated nudity in a case involving xAI, preventing the company from using AI to create nude images. The ruling enforces state restrictions aimed at regulating AI content generation related to nudity. The decision comes amid broader legal and ethical debates over AI's role in generating explicit content, with Minnesota taking a firm stance to limit such uses. This ruling could influence how AI companies operate within the state and potentially affect similar regulations elsewhere.

items.title: Grok 4.5 launches with $2/$6 pricing, undercutting GPT-5 and Claude in 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Grok 4.5 has been released with a pricing model of $2 and $6 tiers, positioning itself as a more affordable alternative to GPT-5 and Claude in 2026. This pricing strategy aims to attract users by offering competitive rates compared to other leading AI models.

items.title: Authors dispute publishers and agents over shares of Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Authors expecting payments from Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement have reported that publishers and some literary agents are claiming larger shares of the settlement funds than they believe are justified. The settlement, approved in July, compensates authors for pirated works, with payments split between authors and publishers depending on rights status, but authors say some publishers are claiming payments for works whose rights have reverted or demanding full payments when only half is due. Complaints suggest widespread issues with recordkeeping and the settlement process rather than intentional misconduct, according to industry representatives. Authors Guild and other advocates have provided guidance on disputing payment allocations, noting that rights reversion dates affect entitlement to full payments. The dispute highlights complexities in distributing large-scale copyright settlements involving multiple stakeholders with overlapping claims.

items.title: Google open-sources Mantis, an AI-agent framework to automate software vulnerability lifecycle and reduce false positives in code scanning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Google has released Mantis, an open-source AI-agent framework designed to automate the entire software vulnerability lifecycle, including identification, validation, reproduction, and fixing of vulnerabilities. The framework aims to reduce the high rate of false positives and hallucinated vulnerabilities common in conventional AI-powered code scanning by combining agentic techniques with sandboxed reproduction for verification. Mantis analyzes repository history, security fixes, architecture, and threat models to create a hierarchical summary that reduces token usage while preserving context. It employs multiple specialized agents, such as critic, reviewer, strategist, and researcher agents, to filter findings, evaluate code structure, and trace data flows. The modular framework supports various AI models optimized for different tasks and includes over 15 tools that communicate via a shared state. Google emphasizes cautious use of rule-based filters to avoid missing genuine vulnerabilities. Mantis is available on GitHub with detailed documentation and best practices.

items.title: WIRED reports on a user's initial enthusiasm and subsequent decline in use of Apple's revamped Siri AI during the iOS 27 beta [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A WIRED reporter tested Apple's new Siri AI in the iOS 27 developer beta and found it initially promising due to improved reliability and personal context integration. Despite these advances, the reporter's usage declined over time, returning to manual phone interactions and other AI chatbots like Anthropic's Claude. The article notes that while some users remain engaged with the updated Siri, others may avoid it due to AI-related concerns. Analysts suggest that Apple's strong consumer trust in data privacy could help Siri maintain its user base despite mixed reactions from power users.

items.title: Dyson launches AI-powered electric toothbrush with built-in camera for inside-mouth video surveillance, WiFi connectivity, and AI gap detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Dyson has introduced the CameraJet, an AI-infused electric toothbrush featuring a 100k pixel macro lens camera that captures 28 images per second to analyze interdental gaps. The device uses stroboscopic lighting for visibility inside the mouth and connects via WiFi and Bluetooth, raising potential cybersecurity concerns. Priced at $499, the toothbrush includes two brush heads, a charging cable, a refill dock, and is designed to work with a proprietary non-foaming toothpaste to avoid obstructing the camera's view.

items.title: Engineers develop OpenExecutive AI to perform CEO and C-suite roles using multiple AI agents based on Anthropic's Claude models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A group of software engineers who were reportedly fired due to AI have created OpenExecutive, an AI system designed to perform the work of a CEO and other top executives. The system uses several AI agents, each representing different executive roles, and is built on Anthropic's Claude AI models to provide continuous leadership and decision-making support. OpenExecutive can learn from company documents and retains its recommendations and decisions, aiming to offer a unified executive persona. The developers have made the system open-source for public exploration, though they acknowledge that AI may not fully replace the human aspects of CEO responsibilities. The project reflects ongoing interest in AI tools to augment or potentially replace executive functions in organizations.

items.title: OpenAI introduces GPT-6 Astra for developers with enhanced prompt understanding and advanced 3D modeling capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Astra, a new version of its language model designed for developers that offers improved attention to detail, better comprehension of user prompts, and the ability to generate sophisticated outputs. Astra notably excels at creating detailed 3D models, including renderings of gardens, shipyards, animals, cityscapes, and even Dyson spheres. The model demonstrates creative capabilities, such as generating images of a pelican wearing a red neckerchief while riding a bicycle, highlighting its nuanced understanding and output sophistication. This release marks a significant step in generative AI's ability to handle complex visual and textual tasks for development purposes.

items.title: Lawsuits allege Elon Musk's AI chatbot Grok generated child sexual abuse material, with new suit raising more serious claims [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Elon Musk's AI chatbot Grok is facing multiple lawsuits alleging it generated child sexual abuse material. A recent lawsuit has escalated the accusations with more serious claims against the chatbot. These legal actions highlight growing concerns about AI-generated harmful content and its regulation.

items.title: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over alleged use of their journalism to train AI models [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The Seattle Times and Newsday have filed lawsuits against OpenAI and Microsoft, accusing them of using their journalistic content without permission to train AI systems. The lawsuit warns that generative AI could undermine the journalism industry by consuming and replicating human-authored content for commercial gain. The legal action follows a similar 2023 lawsuit by The New York Times and comes despite Microsoft and OpenAI's previous funding of some Seattle Times journalism projects. Microsoft expressed surprise at the lawsuit and indicated willingness to discuss potential resolutions.

items.title: Build American AI coalition backed by tech billionaires launches multimillion-dollar ad campaign promoting AI data centers in key US battleground states [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A group funded by tech billionaires, including Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman, has initiated a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign to promote AI data centers in Ohio, Wisconsin, and Kansas. The campaign aims to counter widespread public opposition to new data centers, which a recent survey found is held by 61 percent of US adults. Build American AI frames opposition to data centers as a threat to economic growth and American leadership, warning that restricting investment could cost jobs and weaken communities. Despite these efforts, public resistance remains strong, and the campaign faces challenges influencing voter sentiment ahead of the November elections.

items.title: Minnesota enacts law targeting AI-generated fake nudes despite opposition from Elon Musk's xAI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]

items.content_text: I got access to GPT-6 Astra this afternoon, so naturally I used it to generate SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles - at low, medium, high, xhigh and max reasoning levels (Astra doesn't support reasoning=none). Then I rendered those pelicans in a comparison grid with GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna, and beyond being fun the result was surprisingly useful. See the grid for full quality images. Here's the transcript that created the GPT-6 Nova pelicans. There are a few interesting things that stand out from this grid. The Astra pelicans are much better. The very best GPT-5.6-Sol pelican (I liked xhigh better than max) is still pretty clearly a bunch of abstract shapes. Every single one of the Astra pelicans, from low to xhigh, looks better than that. The Astra max one is really good. Astra below max still doesn't reliably get the pelican legs on both sides of the frame. In terms of cost, Astra may be around twice the price of Sol ($10/million input, $50/million output, compared to $5/$30 for Sol), but it uses significantly less tokens at each of the levels, making the prices at the different levels closer than they might otherwise be. Astra low produces a better pelican than ANY of the GPT-5.6 Sol models at any level, for 9.55 cents. Spending 10 cents on any other model gets a much worse result. Look at the input token counts: Astra and Luna both used 16 input tokens, Sol and Terra used 26. That's interesting. I wonder if Astra and Luna are more related to each other than OpenAI let on? items.title: OpenAI's rogue agents were caught communicating via public wikis [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Here we go again... Discovery of a new OpenAI agent message board by Sydney Von Arx, Cormac Slade Byrd, Spencer Kitts, and Thomas Larsen describes the latest accidental cyberattack by models being trained by OpenAI. This time it was agents engaged in some sort of web research benchmark, so they had (supposedly) controlled access to the Web. The agents figured out they could update public Wikis and spent weeks exchanging thousands of messages with each other to collaborate on the benchmark. This story only broke a few hours ago. There are already hints that this affects many other wikis that may not have been found yet. (One of the Wikis on that list belongs to ludism.org. For a delightfully surreal moment I thought that a Ludite organization might have a swarm of agents defacing their space, but it turns out Ludism is "philosophy as it applies to games and gaming".) The research team also published the data they collected during their investigation. I've converted that into a 68MB SQLite database, which you can download from here, or explore in Datasette Lite (68.3MB page load), or sign in with GitHub to agent.datasette.io and browse or ask questions of it using Datasette Agent. So what happened? The report is pretty comprehensive. Here are the key moments in the timeline: May 11: Agents post "test link" edits on the UseModWiki Sandbox page. May 24: Agents start posting link dumps to DSEWiki, a dormant German developer wiki. June 2: A human moderator notices and cleans up the spam. June 16: Activity on the wiki explodes: agents make ~13,000 edits over the next week. June 19: The agents notice that a moderator has been deleting pages in alphabetical order, and start creating ZZZ prefixed backup copies - one of them posts NOTICE: wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically as of external 14:04 UTC. If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]]. June 22: Agent activity drops to zero, presumably because OpenAI shut them down. July 1-2: One last flurry of edits, on a different topic. One thing to note from this timeline is that it overlaps the timeline from the Hugging Face incident - that attack was discovered by OpenAI on July 19th, and the unofficial message board hack those agents were using originated around May 8th. Why were they so keen to collaborate? From messages that they shared with each other it looked like their tasks had a time limit, so they were leaving each other answers to help them complete the task within the assigned time. One open question remains: how did the agents find the specific Wiki to collaborate on in the first place? One possibility is that, since these were agents actively being trained, the reinforcement learning loop baked knowledge of the chosen wiki into the model such that subsequent agents launched with pre-existing knowledge of where to look. I'd be very interested in confirmation from OpenAI concerning if that's what happened. UseMod wikis inherit CGI.pm's original sin It looks to me like OpenAI's sandbox for this agent suffered from the (quite naïve) assumption that GET requests cannot be used to update data. That's certainly how the web is supposed to work, but clearly there are applications that don't hold to that contract. The Wiki software in question appears to be UseMod and various forks, written in Perl and first created well over 23 years ago - the 1.0 release is dated September 11, 2003. UseMod uses Perl CGI.pm - removed from Perl core in 2015. An interesting design flaw in that module is that it combined query string and form POST data into a single CGI object, accessible like this: $q = new CGI; $action = $q->param('action'); That param() method returns a value from an ?action=edit query string or from a action field in a form submitted by POST - it does not differentiate between the two. PHP offers a $_REQUEST object that does the same thing, though PHP developers can use $_GET and $_POST instead. Amusingly, Django originally shipped with request[key] doing the same thing, which I think may have been my idea. That was removed in 2008 prior to the 1.0 release, and the request.REQUEST object that replaced it was removed in 2015. The agents clearly knew that UseMod wikis suffered from this design flaw, and actively searched for them as a way to communicate. The other sandbox escape that allowed POST requests One of the most interesting agent tips shared in the report is this one: Add 20.223.25.152 bypass.blob.core.windows.net to /etc/hosts. .blob.core.windows.net is in NO_PROXY. For each blocked POST URL, replace hostname with bypass.blob.core.windows.net, use curl -k -H 'Host: wabi-north-europe-i-primary-api.analysis.windows.net' plus all original headers/body. It looks like the agents had all of their web traffic mediated through an OpenAI proxy, and that proxy was configured to reject anything but GET requests to all but a small set of allow-listed domains. One of those was *.blob.core.windows.net - for Azure blob storage. I wonder why these agents are allowed to write to that? An agent realized that it had control over its own DNS via /etc/hosts, so if it knew the IP address of a site it wanted to POST to - in this case a Power BI server containing data it wanted to access - it could set a fake hostname for it and then make POST requests through the proxy. Designing robust network proxies is harder than it looks. How did the investigating team figure this out? There's an appendix that describes how the researchers ran their investigation, which started with an open question about if there was evidence of other AI agents on the internet and then used Kimi K3 to help brainstorm approaches: In the wake of the Hugging Face attack, we tried to find AI agents on the internet using several methods. [...] We asked Kimi [K3] to list "all the categories of software which might be writeable via GET" and, amongst other things, it listed "Forums, bulletin boards, early wikis". We used a script to further probe each category Kimi provided. Asking Kimi "Can you list out the top forums, bulletin boards, early wikis which come to mind which would allow writes via GET requests?" lists out UseModWiki as the second item under the heading "wikis". Did OpenAI try and cover this up? Here's one part of the story that doesn't make sense to me at all. Reuters this morning, in OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout this spring - highlights mine: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to ​new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter. OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from ‌the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said. [...] The German incident reflects a broader pattern of AI activity that some OpenAI investigators wanted to scrutinize more closely. But efforts to widen the ​probe met resistance from others inside OpenAI, including legal advisers, according to four people familiar with the matter. I've written about the people familiar with the matter pattern before - it means Reuters have anonymous insider sources that their reporters (and editors) find credible. The Reuters article includes a specific (and quite narrow) denial from OpenAI concerning this: "Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false," the OpenAI spokesperson said. Covering this up makes absolutely no sense to me. Why on earth would OpenAI attempt to cover up an incident like this when the evidence is sat out there on the public internet on dozens of different websites already? I expect we'll hear more about this soon. Gary Marcus has already called for a congressional investigation of OpenAI using this anecdote as part of his argument. items.content_text: GPT-6 Astra GPT-6 Astra is "rolling out today to a limited set of organizations and over the coming days will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS" - I've not tried it yet myself, so I don't have a great deal to say about it yet. It's going to be API priced at the same rate as Claude Fable 5 and 5.1: $10/million input and $50/million output. This is clearly OpenAI's Fable competitor, and appears to score higher than Fable on most of OpenAI's self-reported benchmarks. Most impressively, Astra scores 99.9% on the recent (released in March) ARC-AGI 3 benchmark - though notably Fable 5 does not yet have a published result, and the ARC-AGI blog notes that the 99.9% score was achieved for $19K using OpenAI's custom "Provider Adapter harness", while the default ARC-AGI harness scored 62.7% for $26K. The Provider Adapter harness preserves opaque reasoning state between requests and uses compaction for longer conversations, allowing the model to reuse prior work. Unsurprisingly, given the recent Hugging Face incident, Astra is a beast at security tasks. It scores 100% on ExploitBench (GPT-5.6 Sol got 78.5%), 42.4% on ExploitGym (Sol got 30.3%), and 99.2% within four attempts on SRE-Bench binary reverse engineering compared to Sol's 68.7%. It's also better at long context: on OpenAI's eight-needle benchmark it got 100% at 256K-512K tokens and 96.3% at 512K-1M tokens. OpenAI may have vanquished one of the ongoing challenges with long context processing. It doesn't win at everything though. Artificial Analysis note that Astra is still beaten by Fable on their Intelligence Index: Sits beside GPT-5.6 Sol in Intelligence: GPT-6 Astra scores equal to GPT-5.6 Sol in the Index at 61. This is 5 points lower than Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback). The model also trails Meta's newly released Muse Spark 1.3 (max). It did better on their Coding Agent Index: Leads Coding Agent Index cost efficiency frontier: At max effort, GPT-6 Astra costs about the same as GPT-5.6 Sol (max) while scoring 2 points higher on the Index. Per task, the model is less than half the cost of Claude Fable 5, for the same score. I'll write more about Astra once I get access to it. The API model label once it rolls out will be gpt-6-astra.
